text: A Business Rule is a record on the sys_script table, and it's the most powerful mechanism this chapter covers. Where a UI Policy only affects a browser form and a Data Policy only enforces mandatory or read-only on specific fields, a Business Rule is server-side script that runs automatically whenever a record on its target table is inserted, updated, deleted, or even queried. There's effectively no limit to what it can do once it fires — read or write any field, modify completely unrelated records, call another system, or block the operation outright. You won't be writing these scripts yourself in this course; that's Course 6. What you need here is the ability to open an existing Business Rule and correctly recognize what it's doing and when.

Every Business Rule runs at one of four points. Before runs ahead of the database write, so it can still modify fields on the record being saved, and that change gets included in the same save — it can even abort the operation entirely. After runs once the write has already completed, and since the current record's own save already happened, after rules are the standard place to update other, related records, like updating a parent Change Request's state once a Change Task closes.

Async also runs after the write, but in the background, non-blocking, outside the user's own save transaction — the real choice for anything slower that shouldn't make the user wait, like calling an external system. The user's form submission returns immediately while the async rule finishes separately. Display runs when the form loads, before the page even renders, and its job is simply to pass server-side data down to the client for the form's own client scripts to use — the one timing type about getting data to the browser, not about writing to the database at all.

This power is exactly why Business Rules carry real risk. A single before rule on the Incident table can rewrite half the fields on that incident, and a single after rule can cascade changes across Problem, Change, and Task records that have nothing obviously to do with the record being saved. A poorly scoped or poorly conditioned Business Rule can silently alter data nobody intended to touch, fire on every save to a high-volume table and slow the whole instance down, or fight with another rule running at the same timing, each one undoing the other's change.

When you're troubleshooting unexpected field behavior, check four things before reading a single line of script: which table the rule runs on, its timing type, its condition, and whether it's even active. Those four facts answer whether this rule could even be responsible for what you're seeing.
